title: Choose methods

blocks.heading: Choose methods
blocks.text:
Evaluate a method by fit to the question, evidence quality, resources and ethics. Direct observation can measure visible counts but not private reasons; interviews can ask reasons but may face recall or response bias. A researcher difficulty obstructs collection; a community problem is what the enquiry investigates.

Applied example: Different methods produce different evidence. Direct counts can measure visible litter, while interviews can explore reasons; choosing first can leave the method unable to answer the actual question.

blocks.heading: Worked enquiry connection
blocks.text: An invented enquiry needs to know when a public service opens and why its hours change. Repeated safe observation records the visible opening times more directly than people’s recollections. A consenting provider interview can explain the arrangements, but its account should not be treated as an observed timetable. Different questions can justify complementary methods.

blocks.heading: Compare collection methods by their strengths and limits
blocks.text: A questionnaire can collect comparable answers from many respondents at manageable cost, and a self-completed form may reduce interviewer pressure. Closed choices can hide reasons, unclear wording can distort answers, and low literacy or non-response can exclude people. Interviews allow clarification and detailed explanations, but take more time and can be affected by leading questions or pressure to please the interviewer. Observation records visible conditions directly and can use repeatable categories, but it cannot establish private motives; unusual times or weather can distort a short visit. Secondary evidence saves collection time and may supply wider or historical comparisons, but dates, units, definitions or coverage may not fit the enquiry. Compare at least two relevant benefits and limitations when choosing; do not substitute a definition of the method for its evaluation.
